title: Hype and the Dot-Com Bubble
objective: After this level you can judge a new technology's hype using the rise and crash of internet stocks around 2000 as a guide.
summary: The Nasdaq peaked on March 10, 2000 and lost over three quarters by 2002; Pets.com lasted months. Yet 5.5 billion people were online by 2024. Split tech from price.

cards.headline: In 2000 the internet was the future. It was. The stocks weren't.
cards.body: Both halves of that sentence are true, and that's the lesson of the dot-com bubble. A technology can change the world while the money chasing it runs far ahead of reality.

cards.headline: The boom and the bust
cards.body: From 1995 the tech-heavy Nasdaq index rose quickly as money poured into internet start-ups, many overvalued and with little to show in the way of a product. That's a bubble: prices far above what the fundamentals justify, kept up by buyers hoping to sell to someone more optimistic. The Nasdaq peaked on March 10, 2000. By October 2002 it had lost more than three quarters of its value.

cards.headline: A sock puppet's short life
cards.body: Pets.com, famous for its sock-puppet mascot, became the era's symbol. It went public in February 2000 and shut down that November, having lost about $147 million since it started. By the end of 2001 most dot-com stocks, including Webvan and eToys, had gone bust. Some companies survived.

cards.headline: The technology kept going
cards.body: The crash hit share prices. It didn't unplug the internet: by 2024 about 5.5 billion people, 68% of the world, were online, the ITU estimates. So when a new technology is hyped, split the claim in two. Is the technology real? And is the price of betting on it sensible? The dot-com years answered yes, and no.

cards.headline: Hype: split in two
learned: Money poured into overvalued dot-coms from 1995
The Nasdaq lost over three quarters from 2000 to 2002
Pets.com lasted about nine months as a public company
The internet itself kept growing: 5.5 billion online by 2024

questions.prompt: Between its March 2000 peak and October 2002, the Nasdaq lost _____ of its value.

options.label: roughly a third
options.rationale: It lost far more than that.

options.label: every last bit
options.rationale: The index fell hard but didn't reach zero.

questions.explanation: The Nasdaq peaked on March 10, 2000 and had lost more than three quarters of its value by October 2002.

questions.prompt: Put these moments of the dot-com story in order, from earliest to latest.
items: More than three quarters of its value
questions.explanation: From 1995 money poured into internet start-ups, the Nasdaq peaked in March 2000, by October 2002 it had lost more than three quarters of its value, and by 2024 about 5.5 billion people were online.

questions.prompt: Level 1 called the internet a network of networks linked by routers. What did the dot-com crash actually wipe out?

options.label: Much of the share value of internet companies, not the network
Most of the routers that link the world's networks
options.rationale: The crash was financial, not physical.

options.label: The packet system that carries data between them
Every website that had started before the year 2000

questions.explanation: The crash destroyed stock value, while the network of networks kept carrying packets for ever more people.
